content: Frequency probability is a way of understanding probability that defines the likelihood of an event as the limit of its relative frequency over a large number of trials. This interpretation, known as the frequentist approach, addresses some of the issues associated with the classical interpretation of probability, which was previously the dominant perspective. Frequentist statistics is closely linked to the work of Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson, who developed the framework for statistical hypothesis testing. Other notable contributors to the frequentist school include John Venn and Richard von Mises. Frequentists only discuss probabilities in the context of well-defined random experiments. In such experiments, the collection of all possible outcomes is referred to as the sample space. An event is defined as a specific subset of the sample space that is of interest. For any given event, only one of two outcomes is possible: the event either occurs or it does not. Mathematically, if ( n_t ) represents the total number of trials and ( n_x ) represents the number of trials in which the event ( x ) occurs, the probability ( P(x) ) of the event can be approximated by the relative frequency: [ P(x) approx frac{n_x}{n_t} ] A more contentious claim within the frequentist framework is that, as the number of trials approaches infinity, the relative frequency of the event will converge to its true probability. However, critics argue that this assumption is problematic because we can only observe a finite number of trials in practice. Extrapolating to an infinite number of trials introduces metaphysical assumptions that some consider unjustified. This critique challenges the frequentist claim that their interpretation is inherently more objective than other probability theories. The frequentist definition of probability is highly technical and scientific, and it does not attempt to encompass all the meanings of the word probable as used in everyday language. This is similar to how physicists use the term force in a precise and scientific way, even though the word force has broader meanings in natural languages, including religious or philosophical contexts. In most cases, the context clarifies whether the scientific or colloquial meaning is intended, and confusion is rare. As William Feller noted, the distinction between scientific and colloquial usage is generally well understood. The frequentist perspective has historical roots that can be traced back to Aristotle, who wrote in Rhetoric that the probable is that which for the most part happens. This idea was explicitly articulated by Robert Leslie Ellis in his 1842 work, On the Foundations of the Theory of Probabilities, and later in his Remarks on the Fundamental Principles of the Theory of Probabilities. Antoine Augustin Cournot presented a similar concept in 1843 in his Exposition de la théorie des chances et des probabilités. John Venn provided one of the first systematic and detailed expositions of the frequentist view in his book The Logic of Chance: An Essay on the Foundations and Province of the Theory of Probability, published in 1866 and revised in later editions. The term frequentist itself was first introduced by M.G. Kendall in 1949. Kendall used the term to distinguish frequentists from Bayesians, whom he referred to as non-frequentists. He cited Harold Jeffreys as an example of a Bayesian thinker.
